problem: Topological-graph navigation memories such as VGM, SPTM and SMT store only image features and ignore landmarks. Object-relation methods such as ORG and VTNet link only objects seen in the same view, so they lose 3D object context across viewpoints. Neither lets the agent reason about which objects surround which places, so image-goal agents often take inefficient paths, fail to recognise the goal, or get lost.
motivation: Animals navigate using contextual cues from landmarks. Describing a place or an object through its neighbouring objects removes ambiguity: a cup near a toothbrush is not the same as a cup near an oven, and fridge + oven + dining table means kitchen. A pose-free topological memory is robust to sensor noise, which makes it attractive for real robots, but it needs a way to fold object semantics and object–place context into the graph.
key_idea: Build a pose-free topological graph online with two node types: image nodes for places and viewpoint-invariant object nodes for landmarks. A learned cross-graph message-passing mixer exchanges information between the two graphs, and a goal- and observation-conditioned attention reads the resulting contextual memory to drive an IL+RL policy for image-goal navigation.
insight: Adding object landmarks to a topological image memory mainly helps localisation and stopping. That is why the gains show up most in SPL. With a GT detector, the attention module picks the node closest to the agent 68.2% of the time with object nodes versus 38.5% without (1,007 hard episodes). Easy NRNS episodes show the largest SPL jumps over VGM (curved easy SPL 45.5→91.0), and qualitative examples show the object-free agent passing the goal, stopping at the wrong place, or deadlocking. The update-rule ablation (hard episodes, IL only) shows bidirectional exchange matters. No update gives 53.3/39.3 SR/SPL. The one-direction variants give 57.8/44.6 and 61.3/45.8; the direction in which object nodes are updated from image nodes is the stronger one. Full cross update gives 62.7/47.1.
method: Image graph construction: a pretrained unsupervised PCL encoder embeds each panoramic observation. If cosine similarity to an existing node is ≥ τi=0.75 and the two nodes share more than 10% common objects (IoU of connected object sets), the agent localises to and updates that node. Otherwise it adds a new image node linked to the last localised node (affinity A_im). No pose is used.

Object graph construction: Mask R-CNN (COCO, 80 classes) detects objects. Each object node is a ResNet18 conv4 ROI-align feature, a category embedding and the detection score. A Supervised-Contrastive object encoder (threshold τo=0.8, trained on Gibson object IDs) re-identifies the same object across viewpoints. A re-identified object keeps whichever detection has the higher score; new objects are linked to the current image node (A_c). Object–object edges come from A_ob = A_cᵀ(A_im + I)A_c.

Cross graph mixer: an MPNN-style module running L=2 steps. First, a goal-conditioned self-update aggregates neighbours within the image graph and within the object graph using learned edge matrices B(e_vw). Then a cross-update aggregates object messages into image nodes and image messages into object nodes via A_c. Residual update networks U produce the contextual image memory m_i and object memory m_o.

Memory attention module: transformer-decoder attention over m_i and m_o. The goal image feature as query gives goal-context features (C_ig, C_og); the current observation as query gives current-context features (C_it, C_ot). Attention can interpolate toward unexplored parts of the memory.
Action policy: an RNN takes the goal/current context features and the previous action and outputs a categorical distribution over {forward 0.25 m, turn left 10°, turn right 10°, stop}.

Optimization: behaviour cloning on oracle actions over 14,400 episodes, then PPO fine-tuning for 10M frames. Rewards are geodesic progress plus +10 at the goal. Auxiliary L2 heads (a progress monitor on geodesic progress and a goal sensor for within the success radius) are added with weight λ to help the stop decision.

setting.backbone: ResNet18-based image/object encoders (PCL-pretrained image encoder, SupCon-trained object encoder) + COCO-pretrained Mask R-CNN detector + cross-graph MPNN + transformer attention + RNN policy, trained from scratch with IL→PPO
setting.training_data: Gibson 72 train scenes. IL: 14,400 episodes (200 per scene) of oracle actions. RL: PPO for 10M frames. Training uses both GT Gibson object annotations and detector outputs. The object encoder is trained on Gibson train-scene object identity labels. The image encoder is PCL (unsupervised).
setting.observation: panoramic RGB-D (12 × 30° FoV views) + goal image + Mask R-CNN object detections; no pose/GPS
setting.privileged: none at test time (COCO-pretrained detector, no pose). GT object annotations are used only in training. In the real robot, depth comes from OmniDepth estimation.

numbers_note: Two episode protocols appear: Table 1 uses VGM episodes, Table 2 uses NRNS straight/curved episodes. Both use a panoramic camera and are not directly comparable to single-view Gibson ImageNav results. The paper calls the 14 held-out Gibson scenes the 'test' split. Table 3's ablation (IL only, hard episodes, printed as fractions such as 0.627/0.471 for cross update) is not listed as a separate entry. Real-robot (Jackal) results are qualitative only, shown in figures with no success statistics. The text claims '+4.1% SPL' over VGM, but Table 1 shows 67.2 vs 64.5.
results: On the VGM Gibson ImageNav episodes, TSGM reaches 81.1 SR / 67.2 SPL, beating the strongest baseline VGM (76.1 / 64.5) and SMT (67.7 / 56.4). The largest gain is on hard episodes (70.3 vs 60.9 SR). On the NRNS protocol it reaches 85.7/79.7 (straight) and 82.5/74.1 (curved), against VGM's 76.7/59.6 and 74.0/50.6, with especially large SPL gains on easy episodes. The authors summarise this as +5.0–9.0% SR and +7.0–23.5% SPL over baselines, and show qualitative successful runs on a Jackal robot in hard 5–10 m episodes.
limitations: Evaluated only on image-goal navigation in Gibson with a panoramic RGB-D camera. No object-goal navigation experiments (acknowledged), and the setting differs from the standard single-camera ImageNav benchmark.
Real-world evaluation is only qualitative (a few Jackal episodes, depth from a monocular panoramic depth estimator), with no quantitative real-robot metrics.
Relies on a closed-set COCO 80-class detector and hand-set similarity thresholds (τi=0.75, τo=0.8, 10% common-object rule). The object threshold was chosen by testing on the Gibson test scenes.
builds_on: Auxiliary tasks (progress monitor / goal sensor, Ye et al.)
